# andesim: a hands-on tutorial

`andesim` is one command that drives the Andes RISC-V simulators. This
notebook teaches it by running **real commands** against the binary built in
this repo. Each code cell is a plain shell command - the `!` prefix (or a `%%bash`
block) tells Jupyter to run it in the shell - so everything here is exactly what
you would type in a terminal.

## The mental model: one run = MODEL x ENGINE ( x TRIGGER )

To run something you pick up to three things:

| Axis | Question it answers | Choices |
|------|---------------------|---------|
| **model**   | which simulators run, and how they combine | `fast`, `cycle`, `hybrid` |
| **engine**  | which concrete simulator binary            | `qemu` (built in) or `vsim:<cpu>` (discovered) |
| **trigger** | (hybrid only) where the measured region starts and ends | `marker`, `pc` |

The three models in one picture:

```
fast    QEMU only        fast (MHz speed), functional only, NO cycle count
cycle   one vsim only    cycle-accurate, but runs the WHOLE program in RTL (slow)
hybrid  QEMU  ->  vsim    QEMU fast-forwards; vsim measures only the region you pick
```

`hybrid` is the reason the tool exists: QEMU runs the boring parts quickly,
and the cycle-accurate vsim measures only the small region of interest (ROI).

> Note: this tutorial drives `andesim` (the C++ product). The retired
> Python `./hsim.py` survives only as the parity golden.

<cell id="cell-0"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type># andesim: a hands-on tutorial

`andesim` is one command that drives the Andes RISC-V simulators. This
notebook teaches it by running **real commands** against the binary built in
this repo. Each code cell is a plain shell command - the `!` prefix (or a `%%bash`
block) tells Jupyter to run it in the shell - so everything here is exactly what
you would type in a terminal.

## The mental model: one run = MODEL x ENGINE ( x TRIGGER )

To run something you pick up to three things:

| Axis | Question it answers | Choices |
|------|---------------------|---------|
| **model**   | which simulators run, and how they combine | `fast`, `cycle`, `hybrid` |
| **engine**  | which concrete simulator binary            | `qemu` (built in) or `vsim:<cpu>` (discovered) |
| **trigger** | (hybrid only) where the measured region starts and ends | `marker`, `pc` |

The three models in one picture:

```
fast    QEMU only        fast (MHz speed), functional only, NO cycle count
cycle   one vsim only    cycle-accurate, but runs the WHOLE program in RTL (slow)
hybrid  QEMU  ->  vsim    QEMU fast-forwards; vsim measures only the region you pick
```

`hybrid` is the reason the tool exists: QEMU runs the boring parts quickly,
and the cycle-accurate vsim measures only the small region of interest (ROI).

> Note: this tutorial drives `andesim` (the C++ product). The retired
> Python `./hsim.py` survives only as the parity golden.</cell id="cell-0">
<cell id="cell-1"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## Setup

Prerequisites: the driver, the simulators, and the test fixtures are already
built (`build/andesim`, `$VSIM_BIN_DIR/sim_*`, `build/qemu/...`, the QEMU
plugin, and `tests/fixtures/*.elf`). If any are missing:

```sh
bash scripts/build_driver.sh      # the driver only
# or, everything:
source ./setup.sh                 # qemu + vsim + plugin
make -C tests/fixtures -j         # the .elf fixtures
```

The single cell below is the only Python in this notebook: it finds the repo
root, switches to it, and puts `build/` on `PATH`, so every later cell can call
`!andesim` directly. (It walks up to the `build/andesim` binary, so there
is no hardcoded path - it works wherever the repo lives.)</cell id="cell-1">

            if (d / "build" / "andesim").exists())

<cell id="cell-3"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 1. Discover what is available

Start with `--help`. The release surface is deliberately small: just `run`,
`list`, and `doctor`.</cell id="cell-3">
<cell id="cell-4">!andesim --help</cell id="cell-4">

usage: andesim <command> [options] <ELF> [-- <engine args>]

Multi-engine driver for the Andes simulators (QEMU + vsim).

run     run one simulation
  fast      QEMU only -- functional, full speed
  cycle     one cycle-accurate engine, from reset
  hybrid    QEMU fast-forwards, then vsim measures the ROI

  --mode fast|cycle|hybrid    REQUIRED  which mode to run
  --trigger marker|pc         REQUIRED for hybrid  the ROI delimiter
    --pc-start <sym|0x>       REQUIRED for --trigger pc  ROI start boundary
    --pc-end <sym|0x>         REQUIRED for --trigger pc  ROI end boundary
  --engine <id>               pick an engine, e.g. vsim:ax45mpv_premium (default: the sole one)
  --mem-size <spec>           guest RAM, e.g. 256M / 2G (max 2G; fast/hybrid)
  --verify                    cross-check the hybrid run against a QEMU oracle
  --gdb                       pause at startup for a debugger (fast: QEMU stub; cycle: vsim JTAG + $ICEMAN; not hybrid)
  --gdb-port <port>           override the --gdb port (fast 1234, cycle 9104)
  -- <args...>                forward everything after -- verbatim to the engine

list    list what is available
  models    the modes and their engines
  engines   discovered cycle-accurate engines

doctor  check toolchain + fixtures are present

'andesim run --help' / 'andesim list --help' for per-command detail.

<cell id="cell-5"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>There are no hidden subcommands: `run`, `list`, and `doctor` are the whole
surface. `ANDESIM_DEV=1` only reveals the internal `list fixtures` target --
for instance it appears in `list --help`:</cell id="cell-5">
<cell id="cell-6">!ANDESIM_DEV=1 andesim list --help</cell id="cell-6">

  models    the modes and their engines
  engines   discovered cycle-accurate engines
  fixtures  internal test ELFs (developer target)

<cell id="cell-7"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`list models` shows the three compositions and what each is for.</cell id="cell-7">
<cell id="cell-8">!andesim list models</cell id="cell-8">

MODEL   ENGINES       NOTES
fast    qemu          functional
cycle   vsim:<cfg>    cycle-accurate
hybrid  qemu -> vsim  QEMU fast-forwards, vsim measures the ROI; pick --trigger marker|pc

<cell id="cell-9"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>`list engines` shows the concrete simulators. `qemu` is built in. The
`vsim:<cpu>` rows are discovered at runtime by scanning `$VSIM_BIN_DIR` for
binaries that describe themselves, so building a new CPU config makes it appear
here with no code change.

- **KIND** is what the selector keys on: `functional` (QEMU) vs
  `cycle-accurate` (vsim). `cycle` and `hybrid` need a `cycle-accurate` engine.
- **VLEN** is the vector register width in bits (`-` means not reported).</cell id="cell-9">
<cell id="cell-10">!andesim list engines</cell id="cell-10">

ENGINE                 TYPE  KIND            XLEN  VLEN  DLEN  ELEN
qemu                   qemu  functional      64    -     -     -   
vsim:ax45mpv_mp2       vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax45mpv_premium   vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  
vsim:ax46mpv_advanced  vsim  cycle-accurate  64    512   512   32  

<cell id="cell-11"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>> This repo has **five** cycle-accurate engines built. When more than one
> exists, `cycle` and `hybrid` cannot guess which to use, so you must name one
> with `--engine` (shown below). If only one were built, it would be picked
> automatically.</cell id="cell-11">
<cell id="cell-12"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 2. Build ONE program for every engine

`fast` runs an ELF on QEMU alone - a **transparent passthrough**: the program's
own input/output flows straight through and QEMU's exit code is propagated.

Historically you needed a different build per engine: QEMU wanted `-mvh`
(semihosting), which vsim cannot service. This repo now ships a portable
runtime - the **vplat runtime** (`runtime/vplat_syscalls.c`) -
that talks only to devices BOTH engines model at the same addresses:

| Channel | Device | QEMU ae350 | vsim |
|---------|--------|------------|------|
| stdio (fd 0-2)   | UART2 16550 @ `0xf0300000`  | yes | yes |
| exit code        | SimControl @ `0xe0080000`   | yes | yes |
| file io (fd > 2) | HTIF command @ `0xe0080010` | yes | yes |

No semihosting and no "which engine am I on" probe (a hybrid run migrates the
process between engines mid-run, so any boot-time detection would go stale) -
one binary therefore runs on `fast`, on `cycle`, and across a `hybrid`
handoff.

The runtime ships prebuilt as `build/runtime/libandesim_runtime.a`
(build it with `bash scripts/build_all.sh runtime`). The compile command
then needs just two extra flags: `-B build/runtime` and
`-specs=andesim.specs`, which together pull in the runtime's startup
code, linker script, and libraries so the binary runs on every engine.
The `say_hello` function and the `roi_end` label delimit the region
section 4d will measure.</cell id="cell-12">
<cell id="cell-13">%%bash
. ./config.env 2>/dev/null     # sets HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN (also done by `source ./setup.sh`)
GCC="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc"
[ -x "$GCC" ] || { echo "toolchain missing - run: source ./setup.sh"; exit 1; }

cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>

__attribute__((noinline)) void say_hello(void)
{
  printf("hello\n");
}

int main(void)
{
  say_hello();
  /* ROI end marker for hybrid --pc-end: the return point after the call. */
  __asm__ __volatile__(".globl roi_end\nroi_end:" ::: "memory");
  return 0;
}
EOF

make -C runtime TOOLCHAIN="$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN" >/dev/null   # build the runtime library (once)

# vplat runtime: UART stdio + SimControl exit + HTIF file io; no -mvh.
"$GCC" -march=rv64gc -mabi=lp64d -O1 \
  -B build/runtime -specs=andesim.specs hello.c -o hello.elf

echo "built hello.elf:"; file hello.elf</cell id="cell-13">

y linked, with debug_info, not stripped

<cell id="cell-14"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>On `fast` (pure QEMU) it prints `hello` and exits cleanly - QEMU services
the UART and the SimControl exit device:</cell id="cell-14">
<cell id="cell-15">!andesim run --mode fast hello.elf</cell id="cell-15">

hello

<cell id="cell-16"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 3. The SAME binary on pure vsim (`cycle`) - no rebuild

`cycle` runs an ELF on a single vsim engine **from reset**, in
RTL — cycle-accurate but slow, because it simulates the whole program cycle-by-cycle in the RTL model. With the vplat build there is nothing to rebuild: the binary from
section 2 runs as-is.

This repo built several cycle-accurate engines, so `cycle` refuses to guess
and asks you to pick one with `--engine`:</cell id="cell-16">
<cell id="cell-17">!andesim run --mode cycle hello.elf</cell id="cell-17">

andesim run --mode cycle: model cycle: multiple cycle-accurate engines; select one with --engine (have: vsim:ax45mpv_mp2, vsim:ax45mpv_premium, vsim:ax46mpv_advanced)

<cell id="cell-18"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>Name an engine and run the same `hello.elf`. It prints `hello` and **exits
0** - exactly the leg an `-mvh` (semihosting) build can never run (see
`docs/archive/vsim_semihosting_investigation.md`):</cell id="cell-18">
<cell id="cell-19">!andesim run --mode cycle --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium hello.elf</cell id="cell-19">

<cell id="cell-20"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>**Why this works.** The portable runtime talks only to a UART, an exit
device, and a file-I/O channel that BOTH engines model at the same
addresses (the table in section 2), so stdout, the exit code, and file
I/O behave identically on QEMU and vsim. The `[info]` lines are vsim's
own log on stderr; your program's output goes to stdout. (Device
addresses and the source files that model them are in
`docs/USER_GUIDE.md`.)

> The ROI markers are RISC-V HINT NOPs (`slti x0, x0, 0x5A0/0x5A1`), so a
> marker binary also runs standalone on every engine -- include
> `<andesim/ROI.h>` and wrap the kernel in
> `andesim_ROI_begin()/andesim_ROI_end()`. PC symbols (here
> `say_hello` / `roi_end`) remain the way to delimit binaries you cannot
> edit, as section 4d shows.</cell id="cell-20">
<cell id="cell-21"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 4. Model `hybrid` - the headline

`hybrid` runs two legs in one command:

```
QEMU1  -- drained state + shared memory -->  vsim
(fast-forward to the ROI)                    (measure the ROI, then drain)
```

The result is **window_cycles**: the vsim cycle count for the region, measured
as `vsim mcycle - qemu mcycle`. The result lines go to **stdout** (an
`[hsim mmap]` line, the `[... window_cycles] N` line, and a `PASS:` line); the
`[andesim] model=... engine=... trigger=...` banner goes to **stderr**. With
`!` you see both in the cell.

The **trigger** decides where the measured region begins and ends:

| Trigger | Profiles          | How the region is delimited |
|---------|-------------------|------------------------------|
| `marker`   | a kernel you mark | two HINT-NOP markers (`slti x0,x0,0x5A0/1`) compiled into the source |
| `pc`    | a kernel          | two explicit PCs you pass (`--pc-start`, `--pc-end`); a symbol or `0x` address |

> The absolute `mcycle=...` numbers are a free-running counter and differ on
> every run. The bracketed `window_cycles` value is the figure you care about,
> and it is deterministic for a given ELF + engine + trigger.</cell id="cell-21">
<cell id="cell-22"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The first three examples use the RVV GEMM fixtures - hybrid earns its keep
measuring a compute *region of interest*. Section 4d then closes the loop by
running the section-2 `hello.elf` through the handoff too.

### 4a. trigger `marker` - measure a marked kernel

`rt_c_v_matmul.elf` wraps its kernel in the two HINT-NOP markers (`slti x0,x0,0x5A0/1`), so
the trigger needs no parameters. This is the canonical example.</cell id="cell-22">
<cell id="cell-23">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf</cell id="cell-23">

[andesim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=marker fixture=rt_c_v_matmul
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)

<cell id="cell-24"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4b. trigger `pc` - measure between two PCs

When the binary has no markers, pass the boundary PCs yourself. `--pc-start`
accepts a **symbol name** (andesim resolves it from the ELF) or a `0x` address;
`--pc-end` is the same. Both are required.

`rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf` is the markerless twin of the kernel above. We start at
the `vmatmul_kernel` symbol and end at the return point after its call in `main`
(`0x1002c4`). To find that address yourself, disassemble and read the
instruction right after `jal ... <vmatmul_kernel>`:

```sh
$HYBRID_TOOLCHAIN/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-objdump -d \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf | grep -A1 'jal.*vmatmul_kernel'
```</cell id="cell-24">
<cell id="cell-25">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger pc --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --pc-start vmatmul_kernel --pc-end 0x1002c4 tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul_free.elf</cell id="cell-25">

the same single `vmatmul_kernel` call. The small difference is where each
boundary lands relative to the marker instructions.</cell id="cell-26">
<cell id="cell-27"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4d. One binary, three engines: `hello.elf` on hybrid

The same `hello.elf` already ran on `fast` (section 2) and `cycle`
(section 3). It runs the handoff too: the `pc` trigger uses the two symbols
compiled into it. QEMU fast-forwards the newlib boot and drains at
`say_hello`; vsim resumes there and the `hello` bytes go out the **modeled
UART, cycle-accurately**, before the drain at `roi_end`:</cell id="cell-27">
<cell id="cell-28">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger pc --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --pc-start say_hello --pc-end roi_end hello.elf</cell id="cell-28">

[andesim] model=hybrid engine=vsim:ax45mpv_premium vlen=512 trigger=pc fixture=hello
[hsim mmap] 128.0 MiB at /dev/shm (free: 251.9 GiB)

<cell id="cell-29"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>### 4e. Cross-check the run against a QEMU oracle (`--verify`)

There is no handback leg, so nothing after your ROI ever runs - what proves
the RTL executed the ROI *correctly*? `--verify` (default OFF) answers it
with a differential check: the same ELF re-runs on pure QEMU (the oracle),
the plugin drains the full architectural state at the ROI exit - sampled at
the exact pc where vsim halted - and the driver diffs the two drains field
by field:

- **compared**: pc, all 32 GPRs, the FPRs, the V CSRs and full vector
  registers;
- **excluded**: `mcycle`/`minstret` (the engines count differently by
  design) and the passthrough M-CSRs/PMP (vsim copies those from the entry
  snapshot, so there is nothing fresh to compare).

Any divergence prints a `[state-diff] field: ref=... got=...` line per
mismatching field and the run exits non-zero. A clean run costs one extra
MHz-class QEMU pass - cheap next to the vsim leg. **Trigger constraint**: `--verify` needs `--mode hybrid` with `--trigger marker|pc`.</cell id="cell-29">
<cell id="cell-30">!andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium --verify tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf</cell id="cell-30">

<cell id="cell-31"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>The usual `window_cycles` figure as in 4a, plus the two verification
lines:
`[state-diff] PASS: 109 fields match` is the field-by-field compare,
`[verify] PASS` the verdict. The oracle's stderr banner shows the sample
point (`pc=...` - vsim's actual halt pc).

For regression testing, pass `--verify` on a hybrid run; the hybrid e2e
suite (`JOBS=8 bash scripts/run_e2e.sh`) exercises the handoff itself.
Details (and the failure anatomy) in `docs/USER_GUIDE.md` section 4.7.</cell id="cell-31">
<cell id="cell-32"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 5. Picking an engine with `--engine`

`--engine <id>` selects which simulator to use. For `fast` it must be `qemu`
(the only functional engine). For `cycle` and `hybrid` it names one of the
`vsim:<cpu>` rows from `list engines`. Different CPU configs have different
microarchitectures and VLEN, so the same workload reports different cycles.

Try it yourself - rerun the marker example (section 4a) on a different core and
compare the number:

```sh
andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --engine vsim:ax45mpv_mp2 \
  tests/fixtures/rt_c_v_matmul.elf
```

A heavier core simulates more slowly. If a leg exceeds the built-in 90 s per-leg
timeout, andesim stops it with `plan step 1: timed out after 90000 ms`; in that
case measure a smaller ROI or pick a lighter core.</cell id="cell-32">
<cell id="cell-33"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 6. Forwarding native engine flags with `--`

Everything after a lone `--` is passed to the engine **verbatim**; andesim does
not interpret it. For simple cases, use the dedicated `--gdb` flag instead:

```sh
# fast: QEMU gdbstub on port 1234 (default); pauses at startup for a debugger to attach.
andesim run --mode fast --gdb tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
# custom port:
andesim run --mode fast --gdb --gdb-port 2345 tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf

# cycle: vsim JTAG on port 9104 (default) + ICEman in foreground (requires $ICEMAN).
andesim run --mode cycle --gdb --engine vsim:ax45mpv_premium tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf
```

`--gdb` is not supported with `--mode hybrid` (the two-leg pipeline cannot pause mid-handoff for a debugger).

For flags that have no dedicated wrapper — waveform capture, monitor console, or any engine-specific argument not exposed by andesim — use `--` passthrough:

```sh
andesim run --mode fast tests/fixtures/rt_c_hello.elf -- -gdb tcp::1234 -S
```

(Not run here — it blocks waiting for a debugger.)</cell id="cell-33">
<cell id="cell-34"><cell_type>markdown</cell_type>## 7. Building, testing, environment health

`doctor` (section 1) checks environment health and is a normal command.
Building and testing live in scripts, not the binary:

- `bash scripts/build_all.sh [TARGET]` builds the artifacts (`qemu`, `vsim`,
  `plugin`, `fixtures`, `runtime`; default builds them all).
- `bash scripts/test_all.sh` runs the full suite: C++ unit tests + driver
  contracts + the hybrid e2e round-trips.
- `bash scripts/run_e2e.sh` (use `JOBS=8`) runs just the e2e round-trips.

`ANDESIM_DEV=1` reveals the developer-only `list fixtures` target.</cell id="cell-34">

andesim list engines                        # the concrete simulators

andesim run --mode cycle --engine vsim:<cpu> --gdb ELF  # vsim JTAG + ICEman (requires $ICEMAN; default port 9104)

  --pc-start say_hello --pc-end roi_end hello.elf
```
